zh.title: 佛教的死亡觀（maraṇa）
zh.seo_title: 佛教怎麼看死亡與喪親之痛？從《愛生經》到四聖諦的原典回答
zh.seo_description: 親人過世走不出來、或害怕自己終將一死時，佛教原典怎麼說？《愛生經》(MN87) 裡佛陀對喪子發狂的父親說「愁悲苦憂惱從所愛生」；本頁從這個場景出發，帶到原典對「死」的正式定義（MN141）、死在緣起與四聖諦中的位置，以及走出來的方向——鬆開渴愛，而非斷絕感情。附巴利與白話對照。
zh.question: 佛教怎麼看死亡？
zh.definition: 很多人來問「佛教怎麼看死亡」，背後往往是兩種很具體的痛：怕自己終將一死，或是至親走了、自己走不出來。巴利原典的回應不從安慰開始。《愛生經》(MN87) 裡，一位獨子剛過世、哭到神智恍惚的父親來到佛陀面前，佛陀對他說的是一句他當下完全無法接受的話——「愁、悲、苦、憂、惱，是從所愛生起的」。悲傷之所以這麼重，正因為那個人對你這麼重要；愛與失去的痛，本是同一件事的兩面。佛陀要說的不是「別再愛」，而是看清這條從愛到苦的必然，並在看清裡鬆開它的掌控。若要更完整的架構，原典也對「死」本身給了正式定義（MN141），並把它放進四聖諦與緣起裡處理——但那是這份痛被接住之後，才需要走的下一步。

sections.heading: 「獨子啊，你在哪裡？」——佛陀對一個崩潰父親說的話
paragraphs: 《愛生經》(Piyajātikasutta, MN87) 開頭不是教理，是一個場景。舍衛城裡，一位居士唯一疼愛的獨子死了。他無心工作、無心吃飯，一次次走到墓地，哭喊著同一句話：「獨子啊，你在哪裡？」這不是文學修辭，是任何失去至親的人都認得的那種痛——理智知道人不會回來，可心還是一直在找。
他去見佛陀。換作別人，也許會說些節哀、他去了更好的地方之類的話；佛陀沒有。佛陀對他說：愁、悲、苦、憂、惱，是從所愛生起的。這位父親聽不進去——他反駁：不對，喜樂才是從所愛生的——然後起身離開，路上遇到一群賭徒，賭徒也附和他。一個剛失去孩子的人，聽到「你的痛來自你的愛」會覺得被冒犯，是再自然不過的反應；這部經誠實地把這個反應也記了下來，沒有把它修掉。

quotes.lead: 一位父親失去了唯一的獨子：
佛陀對他說的，是一句他當下無法接受的話：
父親當場反駁，隨即離去：

sections.heading: 為什麼這句話是真的——末利夫人讓國王自己看見
paragraphs: 佛陀這句話傳到了波斯匿王宮裡，王聽了也不服氣。真正讓他改觀的，不是有人拿教理說服他，而是王后末利夫人問了他一連串問題：大王，您疼愛的公主婆吉利，如果她有個三長兩短，您會不會生起愁、悲、苦、憂、惱？您的王后呢？您的將軍呢？您自己呢？您治下的迦尸與拘薩羅呢？王一個一個承認：會。於是他自己看見了——愁悲確實是從所愛而生。
這裡藏著佛陀一貫的方法：不是要你「相信」什麼，而是讓你在自己的經驗裡「看見」。末利夫人沒有引用任何經文，她只是把王自己的愛，一件一件攤在他面前。王最後的反應不是點頭稱是，而是驚歎：世尊竟能以智慧洞見到這個地步——那是一個人親自驗證過後，才會有的反應。

波斯匿王親自想通之後的反應：

sections.heading: 那，死亡本身是什麼？——原典對「死」的界定
paragraphs: 悲傷被接住之後，再往下看死亡本身。和多數宗教不同，巴利原典對「死」給的是一個冷靜、描述性的定義，而不是一套死後地圖。《諦分別經》(MN141) 說，死是諸眾生從其類別中的死歿、消逝、諸蘊壞散、色身棄捨、命根斷絕。它講的是「發生了什麼」——構成一期生命的五蘊解體、身體被放下、維繫生命的機能斷絕——通篇沒有靈魂離體、前往他界這類語彙。
同時，死在原典裡不是一條直線的終點，而是緣起裡的一個環節：「從生的集起，有老死的集起。」只要有「生」，老死必然隨之。這也是「輪迴」在早期經文裡的實質——不是死後的地理，而是一個只要因緣還在就持續運轉的結構。至於死與生之間的過渡細節（如中陰），是後世部派與論書的發展，MN141 與 MN9 並未著墨；經文沒說的，這裡不替它說。

sections.heading: 走出來的方向：滅去的是渴愛，不是愛，也不是生命
paragraphs: 如果愁悲從所愛生，那出路是不是「不要愛」？原典的答案不在這裡。MN141 指出苦的成因是渴愛——那個一再要求「再來一次」、導向再有的動力；而滅諦說的，是「對那渴愛的無餘離貪滅盡、捨棄、放捨」。請留意滅去的是什麼：是渴愛，不是生命，也不是那份愛本身。

把 MN87 和 MN141 放在一起看，方向就清楚了：悲傷從所愛生，是因為我們對所愛懷著「不要變、不要走」的渴求，而現實裡凡所愛必然會變、會離。看清這條必然，不是要人變得冷漠，而是讓那份「不要它走」的緊抓慢慢鬆開——痛還是會痛，但不必再讓不甘、抗拒、一直回頭找，把痛無限放大（就像經首那位在墓地一直喊「你在哪裡」的父親）。導向這個鬆開的具體道路，就是八正道。經文沒有承諾一個沒有失去的世界，它指的是一條與失去共處、終至不再被它擊垮的路。

zh.mahayana_note: 關於死與再生之間的過程，各傳統後來多有開展：說一切有部與《俱舍論》主張死有與生有之間存在「中有」（中陰），南傳上座部論書則不立中有；藏傳佛教在中有說的基礎上發展出詳細的中陰教法（如《中陰聞教救度》）；漢傳淨土傳統則以臨終正念、往生淨土為歸趨。這些皆屬部派論書與後世各傳統的發展與詮釋，本頁所依的巴利 MN87、MN141 與 MN9 只給出「從所愛生愁」的教說、死的定義與緣起—四諦框架，並未論及中陰或死後世界的細節。各說並陳於此供對照，本站不作裁決。

faq.q: 親人過世走不出來，佛教原典會怎麼安慰？
faq.a: 《愛生經》(MN87) 記的正是這件事：一位父親喪子、悲傷發狂，佛陀沒有給他「他去了更好的地方」式的安慰，而是指出愁悲之所以生起，是因為所愛之人如此重要——「愁、悲、苦、憂、惱從所愛生」。這不是要人壓抑或停止悲傷，而是把悲傷放回它的來處來理解：痛有多深，正說明愛有多深。經文接著把出路指向渴愛的鬆開，而不是感情的斷絕。原典的「安慰」是如實看清，不是轉移或否認。

faq.q: 佛教認為人死後會怎樣？
faq.a: 本頁所依的原典給出的是條件結構，不是死後世界的描述。MN9 說「從生的集起，有老死的集起；由有之集起，有生之集起」；MN141 說渴愛「導向再有」——只要導向再有的渴愛還在，「生—老死」的循環就持續，這是經文明說的部分。經文指出的方向是滅諦：渴愛無餘滅盡，循環止息。至於死與生之間的過渡細節（如中陰），是部派論書與後世傳統的發展，這幾部經並未著墨。

faq.q: 佛教怕死嗎？佛教徒如何面對死亡？
faq.a: 經文不迴避對死的恐懼，反而把它收進分析：MN141 說會死的眾生生起「願死不要來」的欲求，「然而此不能僅藉欲求而得達」——這種抗拒本身就是求不得苦。原典給出的面對方式不是安慰或壓抑，而是四聖諦的次第：如實了知死屬於苦的範圍、追認其成因是導向再有的渴愛、確立成因可以止息、修習八正道。面對死亡，從看清它的定義與成因開始。

faq.q: 死亡在佛教是不是一種解脫？
faq.a: 不是。依 MN141 的定義，死是「諸蘊壞散、色身棄捨、命根斷絕」，列在苦諦的清單上；而經文說的解脫是滅諦——「對那渴愛的無餘離貪滅盡、捨棄、放捨」，滅去的是渴愛，不是生命。依 MN9 的緣起分析，若渴愛未斷，生緣老死的循環持續，死亡本身不終結什麼問題。換言之，死≠涅槃：涅槃是渴愛與苦的止息，經文把它放在修道的成果上，而不是放在死亡這個事件上。

en.title: Death in Early Buddhism (maraṇa)
en.seo_title: How Does Buddhism View Death? The Canonical Definition of Maraṇa and the Four Noble Truths' Answer
en.seo_description: How does Buddhism understand death? The Pali Canon defines death (maraṇa) formally: in MN 141 it is the breakup of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, the cutting off of the life faculty. This page presents the canonical definition, death's place in dependent origination ('with birth as condition, aging-and-death'), why death is called suffering, and the path the suttas point to — the ending of craving.
en.question: How does Buddhism view death?
en.definition: The Pali Canon gives death (maraṇa) an explicit formal definition: in the Saccavibhaṅgasutta (MN 141), death is the passing away of beings from the various orders of beings — their dissolution, the breakup of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, the cutting off of the life faculty. The suttas place death within two frameworks: in the four noble truths, death is one item under the truth of suffering; in dependent origination, it belongs to the link of aging-and-death — 'with the arising of birth there is the arising of aging-and-death' — so death is not an endpoint but a conditioned link. The answer the suttas give is consistently practical: when the craving that leads to renewed existence ceases, the whole cycle of birth and death ceases.

sections.heading: How the Buddha Defines Death: The Formal Definition in MN 141
paragraphs: In the Pali sources, 'what is death?' is not a question left to the imagination — it is a defined term. In the Saccavibhaṅgasutta ('The Analysis of the Truths', MN 141), Sāriputta, commissioned by the Buddha to analyze the four noble truths item by item, reaches 'death is suffering' in the first truth and gives the definition in question-and-answer form: 'And what, friends, is death?' The answer is a string of concrete descriptions — the passing away (cuti) of beings from their order of beings, their perishing, dissolution, disappearance, dying, death, the completion of their time, the breakup of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, the cutting off of the life faculty (jīvitindriyassupacchedo).

Two features of this definition are worth noting. First, it is descriptive, not metaphysical: it states what happens — the five aggregates that constitute a lifetime break apart, the body is laid down, the faculty that sustains life is cut off — with no vocabulary of a soul departing or traveling to another world. Second, the definition opens with 'of beings in the various orders of beings': death is not an abstraction but an event relative to a particular lifetime, a particular mode of existence.

The very same definition appears word for word in the Sammādiṭṭhisutta (MN 9), in the question-and-answer on the link of aging-and-death. This is a standard formula of the Nikāyas: the same wording recurs across different suttas and contexts, showing that this is the Canon's consistent formal definition rather than the idiosyncrasy of a single text. The next section turns to MN 9 to see the framework this definition is set in.

sections.heading: Death's Place in Dependent Origination: With Birth as Condition, Aging-and-Death
paragraphs: The Sammādiṭṭhisutta (MN 9) is Sāriputta's exposition of right view. As the monks keep asking 'might there be another way in which a noble disciple has right view?', Sāriputta works through the links of dependent origination, applying to each the fourfold template of the noble truths: what it is, how it arises, how it ceases, and the way leading to its cessation. 'Aging-and-death' (jarāmaraṇa) forms a single link here: aging is defined as old age, broken teeth, grey hair, failing faculties; death by the very formula quoted above; 'thus this aging and this death are together called aging-and-death.'

The crux lies in the link's arising and cessation: 'With the arising of birth there is the arising of aging-and-death; with the cessation of birth there is the cessation of aging-and-death.' In the framework of dependent origination, death is not the terminus of a straight line but a conditioned link: wherever there is birth, aging-and-death inevitably follows; and birth itself is conditioned in turn — 'with the arising of existence there is the arising of birth.' Link by link, the suttas trace death back into its chain of causes.

This also means the cycle of birth and death is stated explicitly at the level of the suttas. MN 141, defining the truth of the origin, calls craving 'that which leads to renewed existence' (ponobbhavikā); MN 9 states that existence conditions birth and birth conditions aging-and-death. This is the substance of 'saṃsāra' in the early texts: not a geography of the afterlife, but a conditioned structure that keeps running as long as its conditions remain. As for the details of any transition between death and birth — such as an 'intermediate state' (antarābhava) — these are developments of the later schools and treatises; MN 9 and MN 141, the sources of this page, do not address them, and where the suttas are silent, this page does not speak for them.

The definition of birth, and the chain traced one step further back — 'with the arising of existence there is the arising of birth':

sections.heading: Why Death Is Called Suffering: The Framework of the Four Noble Truths
paragraphs: The summary statement of the first noble truth in MN 141 puts death on the list: 'Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair are suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.' Here 'death is suffering' is not a lament but a diagnostic entry awaiting definition and analysis — the sutta goes on to define every item on the list formally.

The sutta also analyzes death's painfulness from another angle: not getting what one wants. In beings subject to birth the wish arises, 'Oh, that we were not subject to birth!' The same formula is then applied to beings subject to aging, to sickness, and to death: facing a death that will certainly come, the wish arises that it not come — 'but this is not to be attained by wishing.' In other words, the suttas fold the human fear of and resistance to death into the analysis of suffering itself: the unbridgeable gap between wish and reality is one of suffering's forms.

It bears emphasizing that 'death is suffering' is a diagnosis, not pessimism. The four truths unfold as problem, cause, goal, and method: locating death within the scope of suffering is the prelude to asking for its cause (origin), affirming that the cause can end (cessation), and laying out the way to that end (path). Death is put on the list precisely so that it can be dealt with — which is the subject of the next section.

sections.heading: The Way Beyond Death: Cessation and the Path
paragraphs: Since the proximate condition of death is birth, and craving stands in birth's chain of causes, the suttas' answer targets the cause. MN 141 defines the truth of the origin of suffering: craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting now here, now there — craving for sensual pleasures, for existence, and for non-existence. The phrase 'leading to renewed existence' ties craving directly to the cycle of death: death recurs because a drive keeps demanding another round of existence.

The truth of cessation is the same sentence reversed: 'the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving — its giving up, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment.' Note what the sutta says ceases: craving — not life, and not entry into some posthumous realm. Read alongside MN 9's analysis: with the cessation of craving, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death ceases. The liberation the suttas speak of is the ending of the whole cycle of birth and aging-and-death, and its point of leverage is craving — something that can be worked on here and now. The concrete road is the fourth truth: the noble eightfold path — right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

A final, honest boundary: the two suttas this page draws on give the definition of death, its conditioned structure, and the way to its cessation; they do not describe 'what happens to the liberated one after death' or what any afterlife looks like. The suttas' answer remains practical throughout — know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, develop the path. This page goes exactly as far as the texts go, and no further.

The cessation: what ceases is craving itself — this is what the suttas call liberation:

en.mahayana_note: Later traditions developed detailed accounts of the process between death and rebirth: the Sarvāstivāda school and the Abhidharmakośa posit an 'intermediate existence' (antarābhava) between death and the next birth, while the Theravāda Abhidhamma tradition rejects it; Tibetan Buddhism built elaborate bardo teachings on the intermediate-state doctrine (as in the Bardo Thödol, popularly 'The Tibetan Book of the Dead'); and the East Asian Pure Land tradition orients the moment of death toward mindful aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land. All of these are developments and interpretations of the later schools and treatises. The Pali MN 141 and MN 9, on which this page is based, give only the definition of death and its framework within dependent origination and the four truths, without discussing an intermediate state or the details of an afterlife. These views are presented side by side for comparison; this site does not adjudicate among them.

faq.q: What does Buddhism say happens after death?
faq.a: The source texts of this page give a conditioned structure, not a description of an afterlife. MN 9 states: 'with the arising of birth there is the arising of aging-and-death; with the arising of existence there is the arising of birth'; MN 141 calls craving 'that which leads to renewed existence'. As long as the craving that leads to renewed existence remains, the cycle of birth and aging-and-death continues — this much the suttas state explicitly. The direction they point to is the truth of cessation: with the remainderless ending of craving, the cycle ends. Details of any transition between death and birth (such as an intermediate state) are developments of later schools and treatises, which these two suttas do not address.

faq.q: Is Buddhism afraid of death? How does it face death?
faq.a: The suttas do not evade the fear of death — they analyze it. MN 141 says that in beings subject to death the wish arises that death not come, 'but this is not to be attained by wishing': that very resistance is classified as the suffering of not getting what one wants. The response the texts offer is neither consolation nor suppression but the sequence of the four noble truths: know that death falls within the scope of suffering, trace its cause to the craving that leads to renewed existence, affirm that this cause can cease, and cultivate the eightfold path. MN 141 defines right view precisely as knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the way — facing death begins with seeing its definition and its causes clearly.

faq.q: Is death itself a form of liberation in Buddhism?
faq.a: No. By MN 141's definition, death is 'the breakup of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, the cutting off of the life faculty' — an item under the truth of suffering. Liberation, in the suttas, is the truth of cessation: 'the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its giving up, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment' — what ends is craving, not life. By MN 9's analysis, if craving has not been abandoned, the conditioned cycle of birth and aging-and-death continues, so death as such resolves nothing. In short, death is not nibbāna: nibbāna is the ending of craving and of suffering, located by the texts in the fruit of the path, not in the event of dying.

faq.q: Which sutta gives the Buddhist definition of death?
faq.a: The fullest formal definition is in the Saccavibhaṅgasutta (MN 141), under the truth of suffering: death is the passing away of beings from their order of beings — perishing, dissolution, disappearance, dying, death, the completion of time, the breakup of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, the cutting off of the life faculty (mn141:13.2). The same formula appears word for word in the Sammādiṭṭhisutta (MN 9), in the analysis of the aging-and-death link (mn9:22.5), showing that this is the Nikāyas' standard definition. This page is written from the Pali text of these two suttas.
